title: MA9-12438
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants are XXXXXXXXX (the principal claimant), his wife, XXXXXXXXXX, and their minor daughter, XXXXXXXXX, all citizens of Pakistan, who claim refugee status pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
XXXXXXXXX has been named as the designated representative of her minor daughter.

The union between the principal claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXX (XXXXX) and his wife XXXXXXXX (XXXX), who are distant cousins, was an arranged marriage agreed upon by their respective fathers. XXXX's father, who serves in the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, was assigned to work in Canada shortly after the marriage in 2006. XXXXX's family owned a fertile piece of land in their village of XXXXXX, near XXXXX in the Punjab, on which land XXXX worked as a farmer. His mother, XXXXXXX (XXX) was never in favour of the marriage as she had decided previously with her brother, XXXXXXX (XXXX), who was the elected Nazim of the village and a religious person, to marry XXXXXXXXXX's daughter because XXXX owned significant property which XXX had hoped to assemble with her own through such marriage.

After their marriage, XXXX moved in to live in her in-laws' home, where she was verbally abused by XXX, who forced her to do menial household chores, because she was disappointed by the inadequacy of the dower provided by XXXX's parents, and by the fact that XXXX's first born child was a girl. While working in the kitchen with XXX on XXXXXXX, 2008, XXX criticized the quality of her cooking and became angry when XXXX retorted that she was always finding fault with her. XXX picked up a container of kerosene and tried to spill it on XXXX who was able to duck away and run to the house of a neighbour, who brought her back to her in-laws' house where she was further abused by XXX. XXXX called the police who came to the house; spoke to XXX and then brought XXXX to the police station, but refused to allow her to lodge a complaint. When XXXXX brought her home, she was slapped by her in-laws for daring to involve the police in a domestic situation. XXXX telephoned to her parents in Montreal, seeking commiseration, but they advised her to be more compromising. XXXXX took the telephone and spoke to his father-in-law, requesting that they be invited to visit them in Montreal, which his father-in-law agreed to. Thereafter, the claimants applied for visitor visas in order to come to Canada.

On XXXXXX, 2009, XXX and XXXX accused XXXX of having committed adultery with XXXXX, a servant employed by XXXX at his home, who had allegedly confessed to the illicit relationship. XXXX adamantly denied this accusation as being untruthful, recognizing this to be a scheme hatched by XXX and XXXX so as to compel XXXXX to divorce XXXX in order to marry XXXXX daughter. XXXXX refused to divorce his wife and his parents threatened to raise the matter with the local Imam, XXXXXXXXXX, and the elders of the clan. Believing that XXXXX life was in danger, the claimants and their daughter left the village and went to live with a friend in Islamabad, without telling anyone of their whereabouts. XXXX and her daughter received their visas on XXXX, 2009 and came to Canada on XXXX, 2009. XXXXX, whose first application was refused, reapplied for a visa, which was granted XXXXXXXXX, 2009 and he came to Canada on XXXXXX, 2009.

During the month of XXX 2009, Imam XXXXXXXXX issued a religious edict that XXXX is liable to death by stoning for having committed adultery with XXXXX, and on XXXXX, 2009, XXXXX father XXXXXXXXX (XXXXX) filed a verbal complaint of adultery against XXXX with the police. XXXX's mother tried through her relations in Pakistan, to resolve the matter, but to no avail. During the month of XXXXXX 2009, XXXXX tried to reason with his parents through a relative; however, they would not relent; rather, XXXXX threatened to kill XXXXX, because he had supported XXXX. Fearing for their lives should they return to Pakistan, the claimants filed for refugee protection on October 9, 2009.
The Tribunal finds that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" as contemplated by section 96, and are not "persons in need of protection" as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act.
The identity of the claimants has been established on the basis of valid Pakistani passports.

The claimants contend that they are "Convention refugees" in virtue of section 96 of the Act by reason of being members of a particular social group; namely, members of a family who are at risk of being victims of an honour crime, by reason of the alleged sexual misconduct of the wife, in contravention of Islamic Law, and whose virtue is being defended by her husband.

The Tribunal finds that there is a lack of credibility and plausibility with respect to determinative issues. Moreover, the Tribunal determines that they are not "persons in need of protection," as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act, since the evidence presented in support of their allegations does not establish a likelihood, on a balance of probabilities, of a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger of torture if they were to return to Pakistan.

The claimants allege that XXXXXX mother, XXX, and her brother, XXXX, beat XXXX and tried to destroy the marriage because it was important to XXX that she combines her own fertile property with that of her brother's. However, the Tribunal finds such evidence to lack credibility since XXX has another son, XXX, single and one year younger than XXXXX, such that it was available to achieve her goal without having to fabricate a story that her daughter-in-law had commited adultery so that XXXXX would divorce her. Futhermore, if it was so important to destroy the marriage so that XXXXX could marry his cousin, it is not likely that XXXXXX father would have issued a threat that he would kill his son should he return.

In her response to question 31 of her Personal Information Form (PIF), at line 42, XXXX alleges that XXX tried to set her on fire. When questioned at her hearing, XXXX acknowledged that she was able to avoid being covered with kerosene and ran out of the house. She acknowledged that XXX never was in a position to set her on fire. Even if it were truthful, it is not likely that XXXXX and XXXX would continue to live in his parents' home after the incident of XXXXXXXXX, 2008, if they believed that XXX was intent on killing her daughter-in-law. At his hearing, XXXXX stated that he continued to live with his parents because he had no choice, since he was working on his father's land. The Tribunal believes that if XXXXX life was truly threatened, the claimants would have ceased living there. In both the written narrative as well as in their testimony at the hearing, the claimants indicated that they only made contact with XXXXX parents in Canada and requested that they be invited to visit, after the alleged attempt to set fire to XXXX, which they assert occurred on XXXXXXXXX, 2008. According to Exhibit A-3, the Memo SIRU dated July 7, 2011 en liasse, on XXXXXXXXX, 2008, XXXXX father, who is posted in the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Montreal, indicated that his daughters expressed their desire to visit their parents in Montreal and asked the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX to approach the Canadian High Commission in Pakistan to issue the necessary visas. This indicates that XXXX had already requested an opportunity to visit her family in Montreal prior to XXXXX allegedly having made such request of his father-in-law during a telephone conversation of XXXXXXXX, 2008. The claimants had no plausible explanation, and the Tribunal is of the opinion that the claimants' evidence with respect to XXX attempting to burn XXXX is a fabrication. With respect to the evidence that the claimants moved to Islamabad at the end of the March 2009 because of the allegations that XXXX had committed adultery and his parents were ordering him to divorce her, the Tribunal is of the opinion that there is no cogent evidence to support such allegation. The claimants have furnished no proof of where they lived in Islamabad. Furthermore, in the Memo SIRU of April 21, 2011, forming part of Exhibit A-3 en liasse, the application for a temporary resident visa on the part of XXXXX, which was filed during the month of XXXXX 2009, while he was allegedly living in Islamabad, indicates that his then current mailing address was still at his parents' home in the village of XXXXXX. When questioned at the hearing, XXXXX claimed that he was unable to change his identification card without the cooperation of his father and therefore, his identification card continued to reflect his parents' address; however, it does not explain why he could not have provided his then address in Islamabad if in fact such address existed. He stated that he relied upon the telephone number which was given in his application, which allegedly was the phone number of his residence in Islamabad, and upon receiving a phone call, he went to pick up his visa. The Tribunal finds such evidence to be untruthful, since the very same telephone number appears on the application for a temporary resident visa filed on January 21, 2009, at a time when the claimants were living with XXXXXX parents in the village of Daduwana, the whole appears from the Memo SIRU dated July 7, 2011, forming part of Exhibit A-3 en liasse. The Tribunal finds that the claimants have offered no cogent evidence of ever having left the residence of XXXXX's parents, therefore compelling the Tribunal to conclude that the claimants likely had no reason to do so, such as the supposed threat to XXXX's life by reason of allegedly having committed adultery.

The claimants have filed as part of Exhibit P-9 en liasse, an extract from a newspaper, covering the period from XXXXX to XXXXX 2009, whose headline reads that the residents of XXXXXX protest for the arrest of XXXX and the Imam XXXXXXXXXXX demands that XXXX should be found and punished accordingly. The body of the newspaper article states that the protest against XXXX is because she committed an offense against the Shariit Law, and also demands that her husband, XXXXX be punished because he was an abettor of his wife's crime. The Imam XXXXXXXXXX also states that the police should find XXXX and arrest her. In the opinion of the Tribunal, this newspaper article is either a falsified document or a planted newspaper article which contains fabricated information. It is to be noted that this newspaper article makes no reference whatsoever to the alleged male accomplice with whom XXXX would have had an illicit relationship. When XXXXX was questioned at the hearing, he testified that he believes that XXXX XXXXXXXXXX had issued a religious decree against XXXX and it was for this reason that the claimants left for Islamabad on XXXXX, 2009. XXXXX was unable to explain the inconsistencies, if not contradictions between his testimony and the documentary evidence which he had produced. In response to question 31 of her PIF, XXXX stated (as of line 74) that while she was in Canada (as of XXXXX, 2009) she was informed by XXXXX that his parents have been able to convince XXXXXXXXX and the elders of their clan about her adultery case. Through the incessant propaganda of XXX, the neighbourhood people, the Imam and elders of the clan are convinced, and so is Imam XXXXXXXXXX. The Imam issued a decree against XXXX that she commited adultery; therefore, she is liable to be killed. Moreover, in the solemn declaration of XXXXXXXX, the relative of XXXXX, filed as Exhibit P-6, he states that it was in the month of XXXX 2009 that Imam XXXXXXXXX issued a religious edict that XXXX committed adultery, and in XXXX's response to question 43 of the "Claim for refugee protection", dated November 10, 2009, she stated that it was at the end of XXX 2009 that XXXXXXXX with the help of local elders and the Imam got a fatwa that she committed adultery and should be stoned to death to save their honor. The numerous inconsistencies, if not contradictions, leads the Tribunal to conclude that the evidence with respect to the issuance of a fatwa or religious decree against XXXX is untruthful, and the Tribunal gives no probative value to the newspaper article, forming part of Exhibit P-9 en liasse, nor to the solemn declaration, Exhibit P-6.

In the opinion of the Tribunal, the basis of the claim for refugee protection put forward by the claimants lacks plausibility. The alleged scheme between XXX and her brother XXXXX to falsify an accusation of adultery having been committed by XXXX was hatched in order to get rid of XXXX so that XXXXX could marry XXXXX daughter; yet, according to the claimants' evidence, XXXXXXX father, XXXXX, threatened to kill his son when he sets eyes on him. It is the contention of the claimants that XXXX would become the victim of an honour crime in order to avenge the shame that XXXX allegedly brought upon XXXXX's family, and it is incumbent upon her husband, XXXXX, as well as other male relatives to restore the family's honour; however, in the present instance, XXXXX does not believe that the family honour has been breached and refuses to participate in meting out a punishment to XXXX.

According to the narrative put forward by the claimants, the Imam XXXXXXXXX and the elders of the clan have staged protests against XXXX as well as against XXXXX thereby compelling the Imam to issue a religious edict that XXXX is liable to death by stoning, and also allegedly forcing XXXXX to lodge a criminal complaint against them to the police.

In the opinion of the Tribunal, it is incongruous that no fatwa or criminal proceedings have been taken against XXXXX, who allegedly admitted having had an illicit relationship with XXXX. Not only have no proceedings been taken, but according to the testimony of XXXXX, he continues to serve as an employee in the household of XXXX as if he were guilty of no wrongdoing; whereas under Sharia law, he should receive 100 lashes and be stoned to death. XXXXXX explanation is that XXXX is an influential person and was able to influence the police, the Imam, as well as the elders of the clan to issue a religious edict against XXXX and to compel XXXX to lodge a criminal complaint against XXXXX, and presumably, at the same time, convinced these same people not to lodge either religious or criminal proceedings against XXXXX. There is an absence of any evidence that either the Imam or the religious elders of the community are guilty of apostasy, so as to forsake their belief in Islamic law that a male person should also be punished for an illicit sexual relationship, and the fact that XXXXX allegedly continues to live his life with impunity leads the Tribunal to the conclusion that the claimants' narrative, in support of their claim for refugee protection is untruthful.

The fact that XXXX waited for four months after her arrival in Canada to file a claim for refugee protection is further indication that subjectively she did not have a fear of persecution should she return to Pakistan. XXXX testified that her mother was making efforts to diffuse the situation in Pakistan in the hope that XXXX could return; however, allegedly on XXXX, 2009, XXXXX filed a verbal complaint of adultery with the police, such that it was evident that she could not return to Pakistan. The fact that she waited for another two and a half months until XXXXX arrived in Canada suggests that without the presence of XXXXX, in all likelihood, she would not have filed a claim for refugee protection on her own.

Section 32.04 of Tab 2.21 of the Pakistan National Documentation Package, being the most recent version of the "Country of Origin Information Report: Pakistan," dated January 17, 2011, makes reference to lawyers' correspondence very frequently containing falsified or incorrect information, and the Tribunal finds, in the light of all the other evidence, that the claimants' Exhibit P-5, being a lawyer's letter dated August 8, 2011, falls within this category, and the Tribunal gives it no probative value.

The Tribunal concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no reasonable chance or serious possibility that the claimants would be persecuted should they return to Pakistan. Because of the lack of credibility, there is no need to consider either the question of the availability of state protection or of the existence of an internal flight alternative. The Tribunal also finds, that on a balance of probabilities, more likely than not, the claimants would not be subjected personally to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should they return to Pakistan.

For the foregoing reasons, the Tribunal concludes that the claimants XXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXX, and XXXXXXXXX, are not "Convention refugees" under section 96, or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97(1) of the Act. Edward Aronoff Me Edward Aronoff November 9, 2011 Date /jt 1 Exhibit A-1: National Documentation Package on Pakistan, April 20, 2011, tab 2.2, United Kingdom (UK). 18 January 2010. Home Office.
